notable_absence.finding: This is the honest headline for this page, and it is a negative result the brief anticipated. The page lists 565 error codes across 25 sections and annotates NOT ONE of them with a version. There is no 'added in 8.0', no 'removed in', no 'deprecated', no 'reserved'. A targeted search for 'Couchbase Server <n>', 'version <n>', 'starting with', 'as of', 'since <n>', 'deprecat' and 'no longer' across the whole page returns three hits, all of them incidental prose inside Description cells ('Index is no longer online', 'Last error', 'The process responsible for synchronising'), none of them a version annotation. The wave's target evidence is therefore absent from this page by construction, and I have not padded the record to disguise that. What the page DOES yield is a small but genuinely useful seam of EDITION information: six rows state or imply an edition constraint, and two of them (3230, 9999) exist solely to report one. That seam is worth more than it looks, because error codes are the one place where a gate is described from the user's side - what you see when you hit it - rather than the planner's side. Two secondary absences: error 10100 gates 'Functions of type «type»' without ever naming the types, so the gate cannot be resolved to a feature from this page alone; and the anchor #note-5500 referenced from the 5500 row has no corresponding heading anywhere in the page, so the note it points at is reachable only by scrolling.

cross_component_finding: The page is a hub that reaches across almost every service - Index, Data, Search, Eventing, Analytics, transactions, CBO, spill-to-disk - but declares no dependency anywhere, because a code table has no room for one. Two concrete items. (1) Error 11011's remedy crosses from Query into security administration and prescribes different roles by edition, so a security reviewer reading only the RBAC documentation would never learn that CE users must be given an administrator role to read system keyspaces. (2) The Server-only note on error 5500 names three separate configuration surfaces for one quota - the Web Console General Settings page, the cluster-level queryMemoryQuota REST setting, and couchbase-cli setting-query - which is the same three-surface pattern insert.md shows for its batching settings, and reinforces that 'how do I set this' is a recurring cross-component question the ontology currently cannot answer in one hop. Also worth flagging for reconciliation: the existing Capella record for this page asserts that the See Also section has no content, which is inaccurate - the section lists the FINDERR() function and the finderr CLI tool in both products.
cross_product_finding: Divergence is small in volume and pointed in content. Programmatic comparison of every error code in both pages gives: 566 codes in Capella, 565 in Server; codes present only in Capella = {2505}; codes present only in Server = {} (none). The single missing code is the interesting one. Capella carries '| 2505 | Workload reporting is not supported in Community Edition. It is an enterprise level feature. | **Reason** An Workload reporting related operation was attempted on a Community Edition Couchbase cluster.' and Couchbase Server 8.0 does not. This is backwards on its face: Capella has no Community Edition, so the row is meaningless there, while Server is the product that actually HAS a CE/EE split and therefore the product where a CE user can actually receive error 2505. Either the code was removed from the 8.0 error set (in which case Capella's page is stale) or it was dropped from the Server page in error (in which case an EE-gated feature's error is undocumented in the only product that can raise it). Given that Server retains the four structurally identical CE-denial rows 17097, 20000, 10100 and 3230, the second explanation looks more likely, and this is worth raising upstream. The other divergence runs the opposite way: Server's row for error 5500 ends 'Increase the memory quota if appropriate. See [Note](#note-5500).' and is backed by a NOTE block giving UI, REST and CLI instructions, none of which exists on the Capella page, where the row simply stops at 'Increase the memory quota if appropriate.' That is correct product behaviour - a Capella user cannot set a Server memory quota - and is a clean example of the divergence being appropriate rather than defective.
version_finding: Nothing to harvest, stated plainly: this page contains zero version annotations on zero of its 565 error codes, so it contributes no availableSince, no deprecatedIn, and no behavesDifferentlyUnder-on-version evidence at all. That negative result is itself worth recording for the wave, for two reasons. First, it bounds expectations: error tables are not a source of version data in this corpus, and future waves should not spend budget mining them. Second, it exposes a structural gap. Error codes are versioned artefacts in practice - the code sets differ between 8.0 and Capella by exactly one code, which we can only detect by diffing two pages, never by reading either one. Neither page can tell a reader when a code appeared or disappeared, which means a client that switches on error codes has no documented compatibility surface. If reconciliation wants version coverage of error codes it will have to derive it from cross-version page diffs rather than from page text, and that is a different kind of evidence from the direct quotes this schema requires. The one vocabulary contribution from this page is positive rather than negative: the minted indicatesMissingEdition predicate, used for codes 3230 and 9999, captures the user-facing half of an edition gate and has no analogue in the current registry. If reconciliation accepts it, the six edition-bearing rows here (3230, 9999, 10100, 11011, 17097, 20000) become the diagnostic index for every requiresEdition relation the rest of the wave asserts.
